parent as in the reviewed commit and its parent: the review then read the same diff against
the same text. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided changes no rule and is not reviewed: a row of the index,
a status of the record, or a proposal's status, verdict and review. A row of the record is
reviewed in its proposal, with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the index's rows and the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it, without
the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else runs on it.

The protected paths are the exception. They hold what judges the work, and a run that can
loosen what judges it passes by loosening it. In Crustify's repository they are:

- `GOALS.md`;
- `skills/crustify/evolution/**` and `skills/verification/**`, the scripts beside those
  skills included;
- `skills/artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md`;
- the Lints and Unsafe code sections of `skills/rust/toolchain/SKILL.md`;
- the Testing, Reviewing and Audit sections of `skills/tools/*/SKILL.md`, and every section
  of one that describes a scan a landing passes, such as `ffimap`'s Binding › Safe boundary;
- `agents/common.md`, `agents/reviewer.md` and the Evolution section of
  `agents/assistant/assistant.md`;
- the `evolution` question of `templates/*/CRUSTIFY.template.md`;
- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, which decides the skills and hooks a run loads; and
- `providers/generic/compose.py` and, under `providers/claude/`, `compose.py`, `spawn.py`,
  `system-prompt.md`, `hooks.json` and `agents/*.md`. A generated agent that changes only as
  its sources outside this list changed is not a change to a protected path.

A change whose diff touches a protected path lands on the working branch only with the
user's approval, whatever its review says, and so does the removal of a `weakens a check`
mark from the record. One case lands without that approval: the repair of a defect in
protected code, a script or a provider's program, that blocks the campaign, once its review
approves it and finds three things. The repair weakens no check. Every existing test of the
code it touches is unchanged. The repair adds a regression test of its own. Such a repair is
put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
user. A
change to `GOALS.md` is proposed and never made, unless the user asks for it, since
`GOALS.md` is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: open proposals are landed
as the autonomy allows, the working branches are offered to the user for `devel`, and the
revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled. The
lessons are reconciled when [Lessons](#5-lessons) times it, and the record's rows are read
when [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) times it.

## 11. The record

The record of what landed, `EVOLUTION.md`, and how evolution itself evolves from it are
[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

---
name: conventions
description: "Naming, tree layout, anchors and test placement of the Rust a campaign generates. Read before writing, homing or reviewing generated Rust or tests."
---

# Crustify coding conventions

These are the shared, mechanical contracts of the code a campaign generates: how it is
named, where it sits, how it records what it translated and where its tests go. The
toolchain, edition, lints and formatting it is held to are [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Naming

The workspace's lints enforce the standard Rust casing below, as [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s
Lints section describes.

The safe surface uses ordinary Rust naming: `snake_case` for functions, methods and
modules, `UpperCamelCase` for types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and
statics. A C name's library or owning-type prefix is dropped wherever the crate, module or
receiver already supplies it, and the idiomatic Rust term is preferred over a
transliterated C one. The filled anchor records the C name, so renaming costs no
traceability. Names that cross the language boundary keep their C-derived spelling, as
below.

### 1.1 Functions

A C function's raw binding is `sys::<name>`. Its safe wrapper is a free function homed in
the owning module, named by the rules above. When one C function has several valid
ownership contracts, each safe variant has a distinct, descriptive name.

### 1.2 Types

A wrapped C type is the layout-compatible newtype `Foo`, named by the rules above; its
shared and exclusive borrowed handles are `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its sole and
counted owners `FooBox` and `FooArc`. A port keeps these names while what they name
changes, as [`porting-types`](../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes. A typedef that
names a type under another name, which its item lists among its `typedefs`, is a
`pub type` alias of the type's Rust form.

A function pointer a typedef declares is named after its typedef. One written inline is
named after the site that declares it, its holder's name followed by its own and `Fn`: a
field's `<Struct><Field>Fn`, a parameter's `<Function><Param>Fn`, a return's
`<Function>ReturnFn` and a global's `<Global>Fn`.

### 1.3 Shims

A callable macro shim is `crustify_<NAME>`.

### 1.4 Exports

Each ported module has one raw ABI gateway, its `ffi_export` region, as
[Unsafe regions](#21-unsafe-regions) describes, whose exports use `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` under the bare C names: the
module's functions and globals that C outside the module references, another module's TU
or a C test or executable that stays, the `static inline` functions its headers define
included. The exports serve that C, which reaches the module through them once it has
switched. A function or global only the module's own C references is not exported: that
C leaves the build with the module at its switch, and its callers are Rust from then
on; nor are static functions and static globals, which nothing outside their TU reaches.
The target's public C API, for C outside the target, is deferred: exports serve the
target's own remaining C alone, and that API is a layer of its own over the native Rust API,
added once the modules it covers are ported.
<!-- TODO: that layer, a C-compatible ABI over the ported public API, is not specified
yet. Until it is, a C consumer outside the target does not survive a port. -->
An export is removed, with the raw binding that reaches it, by its symbol's `port/unexport`,
after the switch that removes the last C that calls it, takes its address or
accesses it. A C test tied to the module that stays, using only its public API, does not
hold an export back: it checks the export while other C needs it, and leaves with it.

### 1.5 Export features

Each module's `ffi_export` is compiled only under the safe crate's Cargo feature
`ffi-export-<tu>`, with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root, every character
that is not an ASCII letter or digit replaced by `-`. The feature is off until the module
switches, so that its exports never collide with the C they replace, and the switch
deletes it, its gateway compiling unconditionally from then on.

## 2. Crates, modules, and TUs

The Rust tree is the repository's own, as [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Tree section lays it
out, all relative to the repository's root:

- `Cargo.toml` - the safe crate's manifest, which also declares the workspace.
- `src/lib.rs` - the safe crate's root, with one `cfg`-gated module per link unit.
- `src/<link-unit>/` - one sub-dir per link unit.
- `src/sys.rs` and `sys/<link-unit>/` - the raw bindings, one public module per link unit,
  laid out as [`bindgen`](../bindgen/SKILL.md) describes.

The safe crate is named after its repository, `<repo>-crustify`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section names it:
a name crates.io leaves free, which tells it apart from the source's own Rust bindings,
such as `git2` for libgit2.

Within a link unit's sub-dir, the tree follows the module decomposition in `modules.json`
exactly, and preserves the C layout as far as the idiomatic organization of a Rust tree
allows:

- each module is one `.rs` file, at its translation unit's path below the C root with the
  `.rs` extension: its TU and the headers bundled with it have no files of their own,
  since Rust has no headers;
- a header module is one `<stem>_h.rs` file, at its header's path;
- the two modules of a split foundational TU share the TU's file;
- C directories become Rust modules: a directory's `.rs` file sits beside the directory,
  as `<dir>.rs` and `<dir>/`, and declares the modules within it, or is the module of a TU
  with the directory's name where there is one; `mod.rs` files are not used; and
- a file or directory name that is not a Rust identifier is sanitized, hyphens to
  underscores, and a Rust keyword takes a trailing underscore.

Where a C layout has no idiomatic Rust counterpart, the tree adapts it in the conventional
Rust way and keeps the C path recognizable. A batch names the `.rs` file each of its items
belongs in, as `src/<link-unit>/…/<file>.rs`. Entities sharing a
definition site co-home. A home may be shared across waves.

### 2.1 Unsafe regions

A module's unsafe code is confined to at most two inline child modules of its file, its
unsafe regions, so that the rest of the file, its native code, holds none:

- `mod ffi_import`: what the module reaches in C: its calls through the raw bindings, the C
  layouts it wraps with their handles and accessors, the owners and lifecycle policies over
  C's allocator, and the trampolines and contexts through which C calls a Rust closure
  back; and
- `mod ffi_export { use super::*; … }`: the gateway through which C reaches the module by
  symbol, as [Exports](#14-exports) describes, compiled only under its
  [export feature](#15-export-features).

Unsafe code is every `unsafe` block, `unsafe fn`, `unsafe impl`, `unsafe extern` block and
`#[unsafe(…)]` attribute, and every invocation of another crate's macro that expands to
one, such as one that mints a type over a C layout, which the compiler's `unsafe_code` lint does not
see. Outside the regions, only the raw bindings hold any. The regions take the lint back as
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section describes.

A region exposes to its module only what [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section lets it expose, and the module re-exports the public items a region defines, as
`pub use ffi_import::{Foo, FooBox, FooMut, FooRef};`, so that their paths do not depend on
which side defines them. A type's inherent `impl` blocks may be split between the native
code and a region: each method is visible as its own visibility says, counted from the
module that holds its block, so that a region's private helpers stay hidden from the
native code.

A region exists only while it holds something. A wrap's items are in `ffi_import`. A port
writes its item in the native code, and keeps in the regions only the C form the item
keeps, as [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) describes; a wrapped item it ports leaves
`ffi_import` with its re-export. The later stages empty the regions part by part: an
item's C layout and C owners leave `ffi_import` with its `port/layout` and `port/memory`,
its export leaves `ffi_export` with its `port/unexport`. A module without either region is
native, and its file carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

## 3. Anchors

The Rust item that stands in for each C item is annotated, and those annotations are the
only record that an item was translated.

An annotation is two attributes on the same Rust item, a doc-comment anchor and a rustdoc
alias:

```rust
/// Wraps `fn::git_repository_open`
#[doc(alias = "git_repository_open")]
pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<RepositoryBox, Error> { … }
```

| anchor | meaning |
|---|---|
| ``/// Wraps `<kind>::<path>` `` | safe view over the FFI seam |
| ``/// Replaces `<kind>::<path>` `` | native Rust translation |

The anchor's path is a code span, in backticks, as rustdoc renders it and as the
workspace's `clippy::doc_markdown` lint requires of a path in a doc comment.

`<path>` names the item as its batch schedules it, and `<kind>` says what it is:

| kind | item |
|---|---|
| `fn` | a function |
| `st` | a struct |
| `un` | a union |
| `enm` | an enum, or one of its constants |
| `fnp` | a function pointer |
| `tdf` | a typedef: one of its own, or one an item lists among its `typedefs` |
| `fld` | a member of a struct or union |
| `glb` | a global |
| `mac` | a macro |

A path is made of names only: the names the source resolves the item by, outermost first,
separated by `.`, as the source language scopes them. A function, a type, an enum's
constant, a global, a typedef or a function pointer a typedef declares is its own name,
since C scopes a constant as it does its enum. A member is its struct's or union's path
followed by the member's name, and a member of a member continues the path, as
`fld::AVOption.default_val.i64`. A function pointer written inline is its declaring site's
path: a member's, `<function>.<param>` for a parameter, `<function>.return` for a return,
or a global's name. An element without a name adds no step to the paths of what it holds:

- an anonymous struct or union held by a named member is reached through that member, so
  its members are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`;
- the members of an unnamed struct or union member, such as C11's anonymous members, are
  named as members of the type that holds it, as the source reaches them; and
- an array's elements are reached without an index, so the members of an array member's
  element type are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`.

An element without a name has no annotation of its own. The Rust item that stands in for
it is annotated with the named member that holds it, or, when it is held by no name, with
each member it stands in for. A type declared inside another is named as its language
scopes it: a C struct tag has file scope, so a struct declared inside another is still
`st::<tag>`. An enum without a name has no annotation of its own, and its constants keep
theirs.

The alias is the bare `<path>`, without the backticks, so that a consumer who searches the
documentation for the source's name finds every item that stands in for it. The kind is
the anchor's alone: a label in the alias would no longer match that search. An item whose
own name is that path, a name of the source the Rust keeps, carries no alias: rustdoc
rejects an alias equal to its item's name, and the name already answers the search. Its
anchor is unchanged.

### 3.1 What is annotated

The annotation goes on the public item a consumer uses in place of the C item, which is
not necessarily the item that makes the FFI call:

- a function: the function or method the public API exports, which a consumer imports
  instead of the FFI function. The private helper that makes the call, an `ffi_export`
  gateway and a test are not annotated.
- a lifecycle routine, raw, typed or string: the method of the public lifecycle trait the
  strategy implements, such as `CDrop::c_drop`, where it is handwritten, or the macro
  invocation that mints it, which passes the annotation to the method. Again, the method
  annotated need not be the one making the unsafe call.
- a type: the layout newtype that defines the FFI type, handwritten or minted by
  `define_ctype!`.
- a union: the tagged enum that stands in for it at every use.
- an enum: the Rust enum or newtype that stands in for it, and each of its constants: the
  variant or the constant that stands in for it.
- a macro: the generic, `const`, function or `macro_rules!` that stands in for it; a type
  generator's instances keep their own kinds, on the aliases.
- a function pointer: the callable type that stands in for it, or the trait, for a struct
  of function pointers.
- a typedef: the alias that stands in for it.
- a member: each of its accessors, the getter and the setter alike.

### 3.2 Several stand-ins

One C item may have several annotated Rust items, each carrying the same anchor and
alias: the ownership variants one C function is split into when one signature cannot
express every valid contract, as [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Functions section describes, and the accessors of one field. That is the only case in which an
annotation is duplicated. Existing annotations are completed work unless the current
objective deliberately promotes their item: a port of an item a binding wraps, or the
`port/layout` that gives a wrapped struct or union its native layout, replaces its `Wraps`
anchor with a `Replaces` one, and keeps its alias.

## 4. Testing

Tests are placed by what they target. Tests of the public interface are Cargo integration
tests of the safe crate, under `tests/`, so crate privacy enforces
the public-interface boundary. Each suite's `main.rs` declares one module per tested
translation unit, in `<suite>/<the tested TU>.rs`.

- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the safe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_safe`, whose `main.rs` carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Those the compiler
  should reject are placed in `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the unsafe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_unsafe`.
- Tests that compare the module's exported API with C's are placed in `tests/equiv_pub`,
  and those that compare its internals with C's in an inline `#[cfg(test)] mod equiv_priv`
  beside the unit they test.
- Tests that check the public interface through Rust assertions are placed in
  `tests/unit_pub`, and those that check internal routines in an inline
  `#[cfg(test)] mod unit_priv` beside the unit they test.

An inline test of a region's code sits in that region, and an inline test that holds
unsafe code, such as an `equiv_priv` test calling the C, sits in a region: the module's
`ffi_import`, for the C it calls. The suites whose tests call the raw bindings or the public unsafe API,
`tests/ub_unsafe` and `tests/equiv_pub`, take `unsafe_code` back at their `main.rs`, as a
region does.

A standalone reproducer is not a test: it is placed with the report that cites it.

`pub use ffi_import::{Foo, FooBox, FooMut, FooRef};`, so that their paths do not depend on
which side defines them. A type's inherent `impl` blocks may be split between the native
code and a region: each method is visible as its own visibility says, counted from the
module that holds its block, so that a region's private helpers stay hidden from the
native code.

A region exists only while it holds something. A wrap's items are in `ffi_import`. A port
writes its item in the native code, and keeps in the regions only the C form the item
keeps, as [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) describes; a wrapped item it ports leaves
`ffi_import` with its re-export. The later stages empty the regions part by part: an
item's C layout and C owners leave `ffi_import` with its `port/layout` and `port/memory`,
its export leaves `ffi_export` with its `port/unexport`. A module without either region is
native, and its file carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

## 3. Anchors

The Rust item that stands in for each C item is annotated, and those annotations are the
only record that an item was translated.

An annotation is two attributes on the same Rust item, a doc-comment anchor and a rustdoc
alias:

```rust
/// Wraps `fn::git_repository_open`
#[doc(alias = "git_repository_open")]
pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<RepositoryBox, Error> { … }
```

| anchor | meaning |
|---|---|
| ``/// Wraps `<kind>::<path>` `` | safe view over the FFI seam |
| ``/// Replaces `<kind>::<path>` `` | native Rust translation |

The anchor's path is a code span, in backticks, as rustdoc renders it and as the
workspace's `clippy::doc_markdown` lint requires of a path in a doc comment.

`<path>` names the item as its batch schedules it, and `<kind>` says what it is:

| kind | item |
|---|---|
| `fn` | a function |
| `st` | a struct |
| `un` | a union |
| `enm` | an enum, or one of its constants |
| `fnp` | a function pointer |
| `tdf` | a typedef: one of its own, or one an item lists among its `typedefs` |
| `fld` | a member of a struct or union |
| `glb` | a global |
| `mac` | a macro |

A path is made of names only: the names the source resolves the item by, outermost first,
separated by `.`, as the source language scopes them. A function, a type, an enum's
constant, a global, a typedef or a function pointer a typedef declares is its own name,
since C scopes a constant as it does its enum. A member is its struct's or union's path
followed by the member's name, and a member of a member continues the path, as
`fld::AVOption.default_val.i64`. A function pointer written inline is its declaring site's
path: a member's, `<function>.<param>` for a parameter, `<function>.return` for a return,
or a global's name. An element without a name adds no step to the paths of what it holds:

- an anonymous struct or union held by a named member is reached through that member, so
  its members are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`;
- the members of an unnamed struct or union member, such as C11's anonymous members, are
  named as members of the type that holds it, as the source reaches them; and
- an array's elements are reached without an index, so the members of an array member's
  element type are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`.

An element without a name has no annotation of its own. The Rust item that stands in for
it is annotated with the named member that holds it, or, when it is held by no name, with
each member it stands in for. A type declared inside another is named as its language
scopes it: a C struct tag has file scope, so a struct declared inside another is still
`st::<tag>`. An enum without a name has no annotation of its own, and its constants keep
theirs.

The alias is the bare `<path>`, without the backticks, so that a consumer who searches the
documentation for the source's name finds every item that stands in for it. The kind is
the anchor's alone: a label in the alias would no longer match that search. An item whose
own name is that path, a name of the source the Rust keeps, carries no alias: rustdoc
rejects an alias equal to its item's name, and the name already answers the search. Its
anchor is unchanged.

### 3.1 What is annotated

The annotation goes on the public item a consumer uses in place of the C item, which is
not necessarily the item that makes the FFI call:

- a function: the function or method the public API exports, which a consumer imports
  instead of the FFI function. The private helper that makes the call, an `ffi_export`
  gateway and a test are not annotated.
- a lifecycle routine, raw, typed or string: the method of the public lifecycle trait the
  strategy implements, such as `CDrop::c_drop`, where it is handwritten, or the macro
  invocation that mints it, which passes the annotation to the method. Again, the method
  annotated need not be the one making the unsafe call.
- a type: the layout newtype that defines the FFI type, handwritten or minted by
  `define_ctype!`.
- a union: the tagged enum that stands in for it at every use.
- an enum: the Rust enum or newtype that stands in for it, and each of its constants: the
  variant or the constant that stands in for it.
- a macro: the generic, `const`, function or `macro_rules!` that stands in for it; a type
  generator's instances keep their own kinds, on the aliases.
- a function pointer: the callable type that stands in for it, or the trait, for a struct
  of function pointers.
- a typedef: the alias that stands in for it.
- a member: each of its accessors, the getter and the setter alike.

### 3.2 Several stand-ins

One C item may have several annotated Rust items, each carrying the same anchor and
alias: the ownership variants one C function is split into when one signature cannot
express every valid contract, as [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Functions section describes, and the accessors of one field. That is the only case in which an
annotation is duplicated. Existing annotations are completed work unless the current
objective deliberately promotes their item: a port of an item a binding wraps, or the
`port/layout` that gives a wrapped struct or union its native layout, replaces its `Wraps`
anchor with a `Replaces` one, and keeps its alias.

## 4. Testing

Tests are placed by what they target. Tests of the public interface are Cargo integration
tests of the safe crate, under `tests/`, so crate privacy enforces
the public-interface boundary. Each suite's `main.rs` declares one module per tested
translation unit, in `<suite>/<the tested TU>.rs`.

- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the safe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_safe`, whose `main.rs` carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Those the compiler
  should reject are placed in `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the unsafe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_unsafe`.
- Tests that compare the module's exported API with C's are placed in `tests/equiv_pub`,
  and those that compare its internals with C's in an inline `#[cfg(test)] mod equiv_priv`
  beside the unit they test.
- Tests that check the public interface through Rust assertions are placed in
  `tests/unit_pub`, and those that check internal routines in an inline
  `#[cfg(test)] mod unit_priv` beside the unit they test.

An inline test of a region's code sits in that region, and an inline test that holds
unsafe code, such as an `equiv_priv` test calling the C, sits in a region: the module's
`ffi_import`, for the C it calls. The suites whose tests call the raw bindings or the public unsafe API,
`tests/ub_unsafe` and `tests/equiv_pub`, take `unsafe_code` back at their `main.rs`, as a
region does.

A standalone reproducer is not a test: it is placed with the report that cites it.

name: concurrency
description: "How much work runs at once on the host: agents in flight and each build's or test's job count. Read before launching a wave's agents or running parallel builds and gates."
---

# Concurrency

How a campaign's work shares the host it runs on: how much of it runs at once, and how
the builds, tests and gates inside it are parallelized. What runs in which order is
[scheduling](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s; this spec describes only how much of what may run is in
flight.

## 1. Principle

Concurrency is maximized given the resources and the parallel workloads that share them,
without lengthening the latency of any unit of work. The resources are the host's cores,
memory, disk and I/O, and the providers' request rates. The parallel workloads are
everything that runs on the host at once: the campaign's agents, the agents of its side
campaigns and of other campaigns on the same host, the shared rebuilds of the target's
variants, and the gates each agent runs.

Concurrency is therefore decided when work starts, from the state of the host at that
moment, and revised as that state changes. No committed artifact fixes it.

## 2. Agents

An agent spends most of its time waiting on its model, and only part of it building and
testing. More agents can be in flight than the host has cores; what bounds them is how
much of their building and testing overlaps, the memory and disk each one's tree takes, and
the rate the provider allows.

The number of agents in flight follows from those, for each wave as it starts and again as
its batches land or fail. A `parallelism` number in the settings' `workload` answer, or an
audit's `parallelism` answer, is a cap on it; the default, `assistant's choice`, sets none. When the waves of several modules, campaigns,
or of a campaign and its side campaigns, run at once, they share the host as one workload.

One unit of work may be given priority over another by suspending the other's agents, with
every process of their trees, and resuming them once the first has finished. A suspended
agent keeps its state; its interval then includes the suspension, and its record says so.

## 3. Jobs

Each build, test run and gate takes its parallelism when it starts, from the jobs already
running on the host: the job count of a build, the threads of a test binary, and the
number of gate invocations run side by side, such as Miri's or BSan's one per test binary.
The jobs of every workload on the host add up to about its core count: a workload that
runs alone takes the whole host, and one among many takes its share.

The jobs actually running are the measure, not the load average alone, which lags them and
counts what waits on I/O. Memory bounds a job count as well as cores do: a link or a
sanitized test binary can need more memory than a core's share.

The parallelism is given to each command through its environment, so that no command
carries it: `MAKEFLAGS=-j<n>` for Make, `CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL=<n>` for CMake,
`CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=<n>` for Cargo, and `RUST_TEST_THREADS=<n>` for Rust tests, or the build
system's own equivalent.

## 4. Artifacts

`crustify/artifacts/build.json`'s commands carry no job count. A job count does not change
what a build produces, so it is no part of a variant: adding or removing one does not
change the variant, and does not raise the file's `version`. The `workload` answer's
`parallelism`, when set, is the only number a campaign records, and it is a cap.

---
name: ffimap
description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB, and, as a hint only, when planning an audit's scope and worksets."
---

# ffimap

ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.

It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```

Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \

SKILL.md
end-gates
test_end_gates.py
usage: end-gates [-h] [--logs LOGS] [--stages STAGES] [--rev REV |
                 --working-tree] [--label LABEL] [--package PACKAGE]
                 [--runner RUNNER] [--link LINK] [--skip-file SKIP_FILE]
                 [--stage-env STAGE_ENV] [--lint-features LINT_FEATURES]
                 [--timeout TIMEOUT] [--parallel PARALLEL] [--nightly NIGHTLY]
                 [tree]

end-gates: run a wave's or a module's end gates over a snapshot of a tree.

    end-gates <tree> --logs <dir> [--stages lint,plain,asan-ubsan,tsan,miri,bsan]
              [--rev <rev> | --working-tree] [--package <name>] [--runner <cmd>]
              [--link <path>]... [--skip-file <file>] [--stage-env <stage>:<K>=<V>]...
              [--lint-features <features>]... [--timeout <seconds>] [--parallel <n>]
              [--nightly <toolchain>]

The gates of testing-gates' Regressions section, run exactly so:

1. The tree's commit (`--rev`, HEAD by default), or its working tree with
   `--working-tree`, is copied to a snapshot, `<tree>/crustify/tmp/gates-<label>`, so that
   work goes on in the tree while the gates run. Each submodule, and each `--link` path
   (such as the variants' builds dir), is symlinked from the tree into it, and the snapshot
   is made a git repository, since a test may discover the repository it runs in.
2. Each skip of `--skip-file` is checked against its test binary's `--list` before any
   stage runs: a skip that names no test fails the run. A run with skips passes libtest
   `--exact`, so that a skip takes its one test and no other whose name holds it. A variant
   stage's skip must also name one test of the whole workspace, since that stage runs
   every binary with the same arguments: a name another binary holds too fails the run.
3. The stages run in the order given:
   - `lint`: the workspace's format check, `cargo +<nightly> fmt --all --check`, then its
     lints with warnings denied, `<runner> plain clippy --workspace --all-targets
     [--features <features>] -- -D warnings`, once with no feature and once for each
     `--lint-features`, such as the export features of the modules not yet switched;
   - a variant (`plain` and each sanitizer but `bsan`): the workspace's tests,
     `<runner> <variant> test --workspace --no-fail-fast`, with that stage's skips;
   - `miri`: the package's test binaries built once on the pinned nightly, then one
     `cargo miri test` per test binary, side by side, each skipping `compile_fail`;
   - `bsan`: the test binaries built once, then one invocation per test binary, side by
     side, each under `--timeout`, with that stage's skips.
4. Each run writes `<logs>/<stage>[-<binary>].log`, a lint run
   `<logs>/lint-fmt.log` and `<logs>/lint-clippy[-<features>].log`; `<logs>/summary.json` and
   `summary.txt` record each run's command, exit status, duration, test-result lines and
   failed tests. A run that exceeds its timeout reports `timed_out`.

The skip file holds one skip per line, `<stage> <binary> <exact test name>`, the binary
being `lib` or an integration test's name; `#` starts a comment.

The job count is the environment's: `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS` for builds, `RUST_TEST_THREADS` for
each binary's tests, as concurrency describes. The exit status is 0 when every run
passed, 1 when any failed, and 2 when the run could not start.

Standard library only.

  --rev REV             the commit to snapshot (default: HEAD)
  --working-tree        snapshot the working tree, tracked and untracked files

#!/bin/bash
# Run cargo against one crustify prebuild of libgit2, instrumenting Rust to match.
#
#   crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]
#
# <variant> is a `variants` key of crustify/artifacts/build.json: plain, coverage, asan-ubsan,
# tsan or bsan. Each variant uses its own target dir under target/.
# The safe crate's build script, in campaign mode, links the variant's static archive (its
# `static` in build.json) into each test binary, so the C runs under the instrumentation the
# Rust is built with here, one runtime serving both. Set CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR to a private build
# of the variant, which carries the same archive, to link it instead of the shared one.
set -euo pipefail
variant=${1:?usage: cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]}
shift
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$here/target/$variant}
# pcre2-sys links the variant's side-campaign PCRE2, the one libgit2's C links, rather than
# building its vendored copy, which would shadow it in every test binary. The side campaigns'
# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done
case $variant in
  plain)
    exec cargo "$@" ;;
  coverage)
    # Source-based coverage on the pinned nightly, against the variant's clang-instrumented C,
    # which each test binary links statically, so that rustc's profiler runtime counts both;
    # crustify/scripts/coverage/ measures the suites as the testing spec's Coverage section does.
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/profraw/%p-%m.profraw}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  asan-ubsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address"
    export ASAN_OPTIONS=${ASAN_OPTIONS:-detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1}
    export UBSAN_OPTIONS=${UBSAN_OPTIONS:-print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  tsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    # glibc's tzset locks what TSan cannot see: see tsan.supp.
    export TSAN_OPTIONS=${TSAN_OPTIONS:-halt_on_error=1:suppressions=$here/crustify/scripts/tsan.supp}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" -Zbuild-std --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  bsan)
    # trybuild's nested cargo build does not finish under BorrowSanitizer, and the
    # compile-fail suite is a compile-time check the plain variant already runs.

# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done
case $variant in
  plain)
    exec cargo "$@" ;;
  coverage)
    # Source-based coverage on the pinned nightly, against the variant's clang-instrumented C,
    # which each test binary links statically, so that rustc's profiler runtime counts both;
    # crustify/scripts/coverage/ measures the suites as the testing spec's Coverage section does.
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/profraw/%p-%m.profraw}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  asan-ubsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address"
    export ASAN_OPTIONS=${ASAN_OPTIONS:-detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1}
    export UBSAN_OPTIONS=${UBSAN_OPTIONS:-print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  tsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    # glibc's tzset locks what TSan cannot see: see tsan.supp.
    export TSAN_OPTIONS=${TSAN_OPTIONS:-halt_on_error=1:suppressions=$here/crustify/scripts/tsan.supp}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" -Zbuild-std --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  bsan)
    # trybuild's nested cargo build does not finish under BorrowSanitizer, and the
    # compile-fail suite is a compile-time check the plain variant already runs.

raced a blob test's `filter::initialise_builtin_filters`, libgit2's `filter_initialize` writing
under the registry's read lock. The two tests alone, at two threads, failed 6 runs of 6, and
the `lib` binary 2 of 2. The race depends on scheduling: the strnlen.h pass, at 48 threads,
passed on an ancestor with the same code. The fix (`67edb478b`) has the fixture pin the
runtime and call `initialise_builtin_filters()` before staging. The pair then passes 8 of 8,
and the `lib` binary 3 of 3.

settings' `sanitizers` answer has it. On the wave tip `4b6e5a4db`, plain passes the workspace

[features]
# Every link unit, so that the campaign's builds, lints and tests, which take the default
# features, cover each one the campaign ports.
default = ["libgit2", "git2"]
# One feature per link unit; each gates its module in src/lib.rs, and src/sys.rs's when the
# link unit is optional.
libgit2 = []
# The CLI (src/cli), whose C links libgit2's: the bundled build compiles its objects, and
# the `shared` and `system` modes, whose libraries hold none, refuse it.
git2 = ["libgit2"]
# Regenerates the raw bindings into OUT_DIR from the headers of the C a build links, in
# place of the committed ones; campaign mode checks them against the committed ones
# (crustify's `bindgen` skill, Build modes).
bindgen = ["dep:bindgen"]
# Builds `c/` as shared libraries in place of static ones.
shared = []
# Links an install of libgit2, found through LIBGIT2_DIR or pkg-config, in place of `c/`.
system = []
# The export features: one per ported module not yet switched from C, which compiles its
# `ffi_export` gateway, the bare-named exports through which the remaining C calls it. Each
# stays off until its module switches, so that the exports never collide with the C they
# replace, and the switch deletes it (crustify's conventions, Export features). None is
# declared while every ported module has switched: those of `src/util/utf8.c`,
# `src/cli/opt.c`, `deps/llhttp/api.c` and `deps/llhttp/http.c` went at their switches.

[dependencies]

---
name: wavefront
description: "Deterministic queries and dependency-ordered plans over the C codebase, the first resort for any question about it: entities, uses, dependencies, pointers, lifecycles, T3 cast tables. Read before querying the C codebase, before planning, decomposing or scheduling, before analysing or binding an item, when packing wrap batches, when reviewing pointer findings or lifecycles, and before changing wavefront itself."
---

# wavefront

Wavefront answers deterministic queries about a C codebase, its entities, their uses and
dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.

It is the first resort for any question about the C codebase: an entity's definition,
fields or signature, its users, callers and casts, what it depends on, and the pointer
findings and lifecycle roles submitted on it are queried rather than searched for in the
source, so that each answer covers every site the traced build compiles, and every query
of one fact gets one answer. The source is read where wavefront records nothing, to read a
body, and to judge what wavefront records.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits
under `crustify/wavefront/`, which the configuration names as its `state_dir`,
`../crustify/wavefront`:

- `codeql/`, the CodeQL database and its T1/T2 tables, and `.cache`, both gitignored;
- `configs/wavefront-config.json`, the campaign's configuration, which every query of the
  bindings and reviews resolves through, with `"t3_dir": "t3"`;
- `t3/`, the T3 tables, one campaign-wide pair; and
- `ownership-store.json`, the findings submitted to it through the CLI. A finding
  submitted once is queried again rather than re-derived.

The configuration's `modules` hold one record per module of `modules.json`, named
`<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after a foundational module's name.

What follows is how wavefront serves each stage: each section names the skill and section
it adds to, and states only what wavefront adds there.

## Binding and porting

Binding and porting read `docs/pointer-properties.md`, `docs/type-lifecycle.md`,
`docs/artifacts/findings.md` and `docs/artifacts/t3.md`.

### Analysis

An item's analysis queries the campaign's configuration, and its findings are submitted
to the ownership store. A type-erased parameter or field is looked up in the T3 tables before it
is bound, and the binding names the type a row gives it rather than a raw pointer. The
instances of a type generator share one generic, with per-instance aliases.

### Binding types › Surface

A type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes, and
submitted to the ownership store.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's record and its users are those of wavefront's function-pointer query,
named as `docs/graph.md`'s Nodes section names it, and the sites of one written inline,
and what reaches them, are as `docs/batching.md`'s Release points section describes.
<!-- TODO: no query lists an inline function pointer's sites yet: they are read from the
table that section names. -->

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each foundational item's lifecycle role is in the ownership store, where planning
submitted it, and is queried for every item of the batch. A role that the item's body
contradicts is corrected in the ownership store, and the correction named in the batch's commit
message.

### Porting types

A ported type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md`
describes, and submitted to the ownership store.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

#### Lifecycle (`lifecycle`)

Lifecycles submitted to wavefront that are incomplete: a releaser, disposer, cloner or
constructor that the findings of the batches that bound or ported items of the type
route, or items of the foundational modules, missed, checked against the lifecycle
primitives `docs/type-lifecycle.md` identifies.

#### The submitted findings

Whatever the objectives, a review checks the pointer findings an earlier run submitted for
the workset: ownership, access, nullability, cardinality and keepalive. A wrong inference
is a finding.

#### Unsafety

The plan cuts the cycles between modules and types. A raw pointer that stands in for a
dependency a later scheduled batch wraps is such a cut, not an `unsafety` finding.

### Reviewing-reports › Reports

A finding on wavefront's findings is filed in its own `<slug>` directory, with its report
and the evidence that proves the submitted finding wrong or incomplete, under:

- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/ownership/`, for a wrong pointer-related inference; or
- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/lifecycle/`, for an incomplete lifecycle.

A defect in wavefront itself is no finding on its findings: it is a proposal, as any tool
defect is.

### Reviewing › Fixes

Under `fix`, each corrected or completed set of findings is submitted again, and a completed lifecycle gets the representations the Rust is missing.

### Reviewing › Plan corrections

A correction of wavefront's planning artifacts is filed in the reviews sub-directory of
what it amends:

- `crustify/reviews/planner/modules/` for a configuration, with the `modules.json`
  finding it follows from;
- `crustify/reviews/planner/chased-casts/` for `chased_casts.csv`: for each `add` row the
  chain followed, hop by hop with `file:line`, or the hop that breaks it; for each `drop`
  row the cast sites that derive the edge, and why they are no type relation; and
- `crustify/reviews/planner/type-generators/` for `type_generators.csv`: the macro's
  invocation sites, conditional ones included, and the shapes they mint.

A report on a T3 table also states the DAG change the edit makes.

## Evolution

A change to wavefront reads its README's Tests section, which names its opt-in CodeQL
tests: a change to a query or a fixture's C runs them, as the `evolution` skill's Changes
section asks of a tool's opt-in tests.

/opt/venv/bin/wavefront
usage: wavefront [-h] [--config PATH]
                 repo_root {extract-ql,schedule,query} ...

Semantic analysis, ownership findings, and deterministic scheduling for C.

positional arguments:
  repo_root             Full path to the repository root. Explicit — Wavefront
                        never walks the filesystem to find it.
  {extract-ql,schedule,query}
    extract-ql          Run the T1 (entities) + T2 (edges) .ql batches against
                        the CodeQL database below the config's state_dir and
                        write one CSV per query under its codeql/{t1,t2}/. The
                        database is NOT created here — build the project under
                        `codeql database create` yourself first. Everything
                        else derives from these tables on demand. Takes
                        minutes — run it only when the extraction is genuinely
                        stale.
    schedule            Order every unit of the config's closure and schedule
                        its `schedule_seeds` with what they depend on, one
                        wave per layer.
    query               Read-only oracle. With no subject, every entity,
                        grouped by kind. `functions`/`globals`/`macros`/`struc
                        ts`/`unions`/`enums`/`typedefs` enumerate one kind
                        (filtered, as a name list) or introspect one (--name)
                        as the whole record. `files` lists the closure /
                        external section file sets. `dag` does the graph walks
                        (closure / layer / scc).

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --config PATH         Explicit wavefront-config.json for extraction, query,
                        or schedule. Relative paths are resolved from
                        REPO_ROOT.

 TSan and BSan have no obligation: the batch adds no unsafe code, no `Send` or `Sync` claim and
 no thread. No raw binding or C changed, so the packaging gate does not apply. Usage cells are
 the assistant's.
+
+### `libgit2/src/util/strnlen.h` wave 225 batch 1: module pass
+
+The module pass, and the module's only review, over batch 0's three paths, for every objective
+with `fix`. It files no finding. `strnlen` is `p_strnlen`'s length for every input: the slice
+is the pointer and its bound, and `CStr::from_bytes_until_nul` is core's `memchr`, a byte loop
+below 16 bytes and word-wise above, as the docs say. It is `const`, safe and anchored
+`Replaces` `mac::p_strnlen` with its alias, and no Rust in the crate counts a bounded length by
+hand. The equivalence tests reach C's expansion through `git__strndup`, which `StrFree::dup_prefix`
+calls on its own copy of the bytes. No C test references the macro, and the ownership store
+holds nothing on it. Porting the macro once is sound under `porting-symbols`' Macros section:
+the body computes on its arguments alone, both branches give the same length, and libc's
+`strnlen` takes its `std` route. The pass adds that evidence to
+`crustify/evolution/config-branches-of-one-result`, which stays open.
+
+Gates ran on `end-gates` snapshots under the worktree's `crustify/tmp/`, at 48 jobs, the four
+`indexer.c` BSan skips checked against each binary's `--list`. On the wave tip `7ef895eb2`:
+plain passes the whole workspace (`lib` 840, `equiv` 528, `ub_safe` 762, `ub_unsafe` 120,
+`unit_pub` 67, `hidden_symbols` 1, doctests 72 and 378). ASan+UBSan and TSan pass it too, except
+the known `compile_fail` snapshots and the `CommitBuilder` doctest. Miri passes every binary
+(`lib` 392, `ub_safe` 194, `equiv` 38, `unit_pub` 32, `ub_unsafe` 19 passed, the rest marked).
+BSan passes `lib` 833, `ub_safe` 757, `ub_unsafe` 120 and `hidden_symbols`, but times out at
+5400 s on `unit_pub` and `equiv`, each on one of this module's sweeps,
+`every_nul_position_in_every_bound` and `every_nul_position_matches_the_c`, every other test of
+both having passed. Alone, the `unit_pub` sweep kept one core busy as its memory grew about
+8 MB/s: BorrowSanitizer's cost per access to one buffer grows with its borrow history (its
+second word offset took 420 s against the first's 90 s, flat at 103 s with a buffer per offset;
+`crustify/evolution/bsan-borrow-history-grows`). The fix, `095f69596`, gives each offset its
+own buffer, and under `cfg(bsan)` sweeps bounds up to 24 bytes, past `memchr`'s 16. Every other
+build sweeps to 70. On `095f69596` plain, ASan+UBSan, TSan and Miri give the tip's results,
+and BSan passes `unit_pub` (67, 71 s) and `equiv` (519, 8 ignored under BSan as before, the
+indexer skip, 3246 s). The diff touches those two binaries' test files alone, so BSan's other
+binaries keep the tip's results.
+
+The safety audit scan (ffimap `9aa2ef1`, flags as batch 0's) differs from batch 0's only in
+`code.tests.loc.total` (`+2`), which moves the Overview's tests LoC. `ffimap api`: `src/` is
+unchanged from the tip, so one rustdoc JSON (nightly `2026-10-08`, ffibox's with private items)
+serves both sides: `mac::p_strnlen` and every unattributed module are `kept`. Coverage was not
+measured again: only the BSan build runs the tests differently, and the coverage cells stand as
+batch 0 measured them. No raw binding or C changed, so the packaging gate does not apply.
+
+Proposals: `bsan-sized-tests` (testing-gates: a test BSan cannot finish is sized for it, on
+crustify's `libgit2-crustify/evolution/bsan-sized-tests` at `6336c30`, awaiting review) and
+`bsan-borrow-history-grows` (BorrowSanitizer, upstream, with its reproducer). Usage cells are
+the assistant's.

# Evolution record

The record of what [`evolution`](../SKILL.md) landed, and what evolution learns from it.

## 1. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. A row gives the campaign and proposal the change came
from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence signal
and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change no
proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came from.
A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.

A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
  it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

class: nit
evidence: failing trybuild test (`ub_safe`'s `compile_fail`: 9 `mismatch`)
conditions: the sanitizer variants' toolchain, `nightly-2026-10-08` (`asan-ubsan`, `tsan`), against expectations recorded on the pinned stable, 1.100.0; reproduces on `3ed770062`

# Nine `compile_fail` expectations hold on the pinned stable only

**Where.** `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/`, on `3ed770062`:

- the std-source notes: `checkout_notify_callback_not_send`,
  `checkout_perfdata_callback_not_send`, `checkout_progress_callback_not_send`,
  `progress_callback_not_send`, `diff_parse_options_no_raw_conversion` and
  `odb_options_no_raw_conversion`;
- the closure lifetimes: `checkout_notification_outlives_call`,
  `checkout_perfdata_outlives_call` and `checkout_progress_path_outlives_call`.

**What is wrong.** The plain variant runs the suite on the pinned stable and the sanitizer
variants on the pinned nightly; the expectations were recorded on stable, and nine read
differently on the nightly, so the suite's one test fails under both sanitizer variants. Two
causes:

- The first six reach a bound or an associated function of the standard library
  (`thread::Scope::spawn`'s `Send`, `From::from`). The nightly has `rust-src`, which `-Zbuild-std`
  needs for TSan, so its notes quote the library's source; stable has none, so its notes
  stop at the path. The rejection is the same on both.
- The last three pass `new` a closure that takes its argument at an outer lifetime `'k`.
  Stable reports E0521 (`kept` escapes) and two "implementation of `FnMut` is not general
  enough"; the nightly reports E0277 ("expected an `FnMut(CheckoutNotification<'_>)` closure,
  found ... `fn(CheckoutNotification<'k>)`"). Both reject the closure at `new`'s higher-ranked
  bound, for the reason each case names.

**Reproduce.**

```
crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh plain test --test ub_safe -- --exact compile_fail       # ok
crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh asan-ubsan test --test ub_safe -- --exact compile_fail  # FAILED, 9 mismatch
```

on `3ed770062`; logs of this run: 198 `ok` plain, 188 `ok` and 9 `mismatch` under ASan+UBSan.

**Fix.** The six reach the bound through a local function in the case itself:
`fn send<T: Send>(_: T) {}` and `send(callback)` in place of the scoped thread, and
`fn from_raw<T: From<sys::git_…>>(raw) -> T` in place of `DiffParseOptions::from(raw)`. Each
proves the same property, `!Send` or no `From` of the raw type, now stated as the trait bound
it is, and reads alike on both toolchains (`rustc` output compared byte for byte against
each variant's built crate, then trybuild).

The three cannot read alike without losing what they prove: a closure annotated `'_` is
higher-ranked and fails in its own body whatever `new` accepts, so it no longer tests `new`.
Each is written once under `compile_fail/toolchain/` and linked from `stable/` and `nightly/`,
which hold each toolchain's full expectation; `compile_fail` checks the directory of the
channel `rustc -vV` reports for the compiler trybuild's cargo runs (`RUSTC`, else `rustc`, as
cargo resolves it). Every expectation is still checked in full on each toolchain. The
directory's `README.md` says how a case is kept toolchain-neutral and how the two sets are
recorded.

**Tiers.** Caught by a wave's end gates under the sanitizer variants, recorded since as one
of "the known nightly failures". The batches that wrote each case ran it on stable alone, as
their gates have them: an escape. That a batch's own `compile_fail` cases are not run on the
nightly that the sanitizer variants use is the gap that let them land.

1	//! `src/util/cc-compat.h`: the compiler compatibility macros libgit2 builds with, ported to
2	//! Rust.
3	//!
4	//! The header has no translation unit and no state: its five scheduled items are native
5	//! Rust, reached by no C, so the module has no unsafe regions and no exports. Each macro
6	//! stays in the header for the C that still expands it, as porting's Macros section keeps a
7	//! header's macro, and its C and Rust forms are not linked:
8	//!
9	//! - `GIT_UNUSED`, in the bodies of 338 functions of the library, the CLI and the tests, whose
10	//!   parameters a signature requires and the body ignores: [`unused`];
11	//! - `PRIdZ`, `PRIuZ` and `PRIxZ`, in the format strings of 26 TUs under `src/`, among them
12	//!   `odb.c`, `tree-cache.c`, `futils.c`, `util.c` and the CLI's, of the clar harness's
13	//!   `clar_libgit2.c` and of 54 test files: [`PRI_DZ`], [`PRI_UZ`] and [`PRI_XZ`]; and
14	//! - `va_copy`, in `str.c`'s `git_str_vprintf`, which every printf-style setter, such as
15	//!   `git_error_set`, formats through: [`va_copy`].
16	//!
17	//! Each is defined, on this build, by the branch the header takes under clang on Linux at
18	//! `-std=c90`: `__GNUC__` is defined, `_MSC_VER` and `__MINGW32__` are not, and `<stdarg.h>`
19	//! defines `__va_copy` but, in strict C90, not `va_copy`. Every item documents the branches
20	//! the build does not take, which compute what this one does.
21	//!
22	//! The header's other definitions are not API, and no module owns them: the attribute
23	//! macros `GIT_FLEX_ARRAY`, `GIT_ALIGN`, `GIT_UNUSED_ARG` and `GIT_UNUSED_FUNCTION`, MSVC's
24	//! warning pragmas and its `bool`, `true` and `false`, which elsewhere are `<stdbool.h>`'s,
25	//! that is Rust's `bool`. `PRIXZ` and `PRId64`, which no C of this build expands, are not
26	//! scheduled.
27	#![forbid(unsafe_code)]
28	
29	use core::fmt;

# The provisional lesson `cmake-property-naming-a-removed-source` takes in the switch that removes a directory's last source

**Where.** `crustify/LESSONS.md`, `cmake-property-naming-a-removed-source`, added on
2026-11-14 from `module-switch-procedure`'s item 13: its Scope, "the switches of
`deps/llhttp/*.c`", and its last sentence, "The dangling name stays until the last file the
property names goes".

**What is wrong.** The rule (leave a `CMakeLists.txt` that names the removed source only in
a source-file property unchanged) holds for `api.c`'s and `http.c`'s switches, as its
evidence shows: gen3 and gen5 configured and built, and gen5's `build.ninja` in every variant
still compiles `llhttp.c` with the property's flags. Its scope also takes in
`deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s switch, the directory's last C source. There the directory's
`file(GLOB SRC_LLHTTP "*.c" "*.h")` leaves `llhttp.h` alone, `add_library(llhttp OBJECT …)`
has nothing to compile, and CMake fails to generate. That switch must edit CMake, which the
rule says no switch in its scope does. The lesson it extends, "A libgit2 module's switch
removes its file from `c/` and changes no CMake file" (scope: every later module's switch),
has the same gap, at the switch that removes any directory's last source. That entry is not
provisional, so it is left for the next reconciliation of the lessons.

**Reproduce.**

```
d=$(mktemp -d) && git -C c archive 230c9dbdb | tar -x -C $d && cp -r $d $d-drop && rm $d-drop/deps/llhttp/llhttp.c
for s in $d $d-drop; do cmake -S $s -B $s-b -G Ninja -DUSE_HTTPS=OpenSSL -DUSE_SHA1=builtin \
  -DUSE_SHA256=HTTPS -DUSE_HTTP_PARSER=builtin -DUSE_SSH=OFF -DBUILD_TESTS=OFF -DBUILD_CLI=OFF \
  -DLIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY=/nonexistent.a; echo "rc=$?"; done

# `PRI_DZ`, `PRI_UZ` and `PRI_XZ` take one of the header's branches for every target

**Where.** `src/libgit2/src/util/cc_compat_h.rs`, `PRI_DZ`, `PRI_UZ` and `PRI_XZ`, the ports of
`mac::PRIdZ`, `mac::PRIuZ` and `mac::PRIxZ`, landed by `wave-219/batch-0` (`f570d2a4e`).

**What is wrong.** `src/util/cc-compat.h` defines the three formats by configuration: under
`_MSC_VER` or `__MINGW32__`, `"I64d"`, `"I64u"` and `"I64x"` where `SIZE_MAX == ULLONG_MAX` and
`"Id"`, `"Iu"` and `"Ix"` otherwise, and `"zd"`, `"zu"` and `"zx"` elsewhere. The port defined
each as this build's string for every target, and its docs said the other branches "format the
same values". `porting-symbols`' Macros section ports a macro whose expansion depends on the
configuration once only "where every configuration's expansion computes the same result for
every input". These branches compute different strings, and the strings are not
interchangeable: a Rust format would carry `"zu"` to the Windows C library the header avoids
it on. The conditions are ones Rust's `cfg` sees (`windows`, `target_pointer_width`), so
`binding-symbols`' shim, for a configuration "which the Rust does not see", does not apply
either: the port reimplements every branch.

No consumer of this crate observes it today. The crate builds and tests on Linux alone, where
the header and the constants agree, as `tests/equiv`'s `the_formats_are_the_headers` checks.

**Evidence.** The header, preprocessed for each target with clang's freestanding headers:

```
printf '#include <stdint.h>\n#include <limits.h>\n#include "cc-compat.h"\nconst char *d = PRIdZ, *u = PRIuZ, *x = PRIxZ;\n' > w.c
for t in x86_64-pc-windows-msvc i686-pc-windows-msvc x86_64-w64-mingw32 i686-w64-mingw32 x86_64-pc-linux-gnu aarch64-apple-darwin; do
  echo "$t: $(clang --target=$t -ffreestanding -E -Ic/src/util w.c | tail -1)"; done
```

```
x86_64-pc-windows-msvc: const char *d = "I64d", *u = "I64u", *x = "I64x";
i686-pc-windows-msvc: const char *d = "Id", *u = "Iu", *x = "Ix";

# A macro whose configured branches differ, under conditions Rust's `cfg` sees, has no route

Status: `open`.

Goal: Equivalence: the Rust keeps what the C computes on every configuration the C does.
Its measure is the differences found after the comparison ended, here by a review. Also
Consistency: two runs that meet such a macro should port it the same way.

## Signal

The recurrence signal of a watched row of the record, `config-branches-of-one-result`
(crustify `769d102`): "a task message or plan correction that settles again whether a
configuration-dependent macro is ported or shimmed". The landed rule covers a macro whose
branches compute one result, which it ports once. It covers a macro whose branches differ
only where the condition is one "the Rust does not see" (`binding-symbols`' shim). It gives
no route for branches that differ under a condition Rust's own `cfg` tests, such as the
target's OS or pointer width. The translator ported such a macro once, with this build's
branch. Its review's task message asked for that judgment "above all", and the review had to
work out the route by hand.

## Evidence

`wave-219/batch-0` (`src/util/cc-compat.h`, `f570d2a4e`) ported `PRIdZ`, `PRIuZ` and `PRIxZ`
as `&str` constants holding this build's `"zd"`, `"zu"` and `"zx"`, for every target. Its
docs said the header's other branches, `"I64d"` / `"Id"` and the rest under `_MSC_VER` or
`__MINGW32__`, "format the same values". Its module pass, `wave-219/batch-1`, filed
`misc/size-formats-ported-with-one-branch`, as its review reads the spec:

- `porting-symbols`' Macros section ports a configuration-dependent macro once "where every
  configuration's expansion computes the same result for every input". The strings differ,
  so that sentence does not apply. Its next sentence, "Only one whose branches differ in what
  they compute keeps the shim `binding-symbols` gives it", then sends the macro to a shim.
- `binding-symbols`' Macros section gives the shim only to a macro whose configuration "the
  Rust does not see". `cfg(windows)` and `cfg(target_pointer_width = "64")` see these
  conditions. The constants are not callable either, so `crustify_<NAME>` does not fit them.

Neither section says what such a macro becomes. The review reimplemented every branch in a
`cfg!`-selected table, which reproduces the header's expansion on every Windows and
non-Windows target. It checked this with `clang --target=<t> -E` against a constant
assertion per target.

## Destination

The spec: `porting-symbols`' Macros section (`skills/rust/porting/symbols/SKILL.md`), not a
protected path. The reviewer does not evolve `porting-symbols`, so the change is proposed.

## Change

In the Macros section's second paragraph, after "and its documentation names the branches
the build does not take.", insert:

> One whose branches compute different results under conditions Rust's own `cfg` tests,
> such as the target's operating system or pointer width, is ported with every branch, each
> under the `cfg` that stands for its condition, so that it computes on each target what the
> C computes there.

The paragraph's last sentence, "Only one whose branches differ in what they compute keeps the
shim", then reads "Only one whose branches differ under a configuration the Rust does not see
keeps the shim".

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a macro whose configured branches differ under conditions Rust's `cfg` tests is ported with every branch under its `cfg`; only one whose configuration Rust does not see keeps the shim | `libgit2-crustify`, `config-branches-rust-cfg` | — | a port took one branch of a macro whose branches differ by target OS, and its review worked out by hand that the rule gave no route | a review finding of a macro ported with one branch of several that differ, or a task message or plan correction that settles how such a macro is ported | — |

The row `config-branches-of-one-result` is `recurred` by this proposal's evidence.

## Validation

Not run as a rerun of the batch. The review's fix is the change applied to the item its
evidence came from: on `wave-219/batch-1`'s tree, the constants match the header's
preprocessed expansion for `x86_64`/`i686` `pc-windows-msvc` and `pc-windows-gnu`, and for
`x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`. On `f570d2a4e`, `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` fails the same check.

## Review

None yet.
